title: Monte Carlo Probability Workbench
summary: Model a practical problem, check its assumptions and compare decisions with Monte Carlo simulation. Groups 1 to 7 of 10: the 10 discrete, 13 continuous and 16 positive, heavy-tailed and extreme-value laws (lognormal to stable, GEV, GPD, Gumbel and reverse Weibull), each with a behaviour experiment and three workflows of its own; censored observations; finite mixtures, compound Poisson, empirical, kernel density and truncated laws; custom laws from a PDF, PMF, table, CDF, quantile function, MGF or characteristic function, each with checks that show checked, failed or unverified and samplers labelled exact, approximate or unavailable; tail plots and the exact laws of maxima and sums; independent sampling, the inverse transform and rejection sampling; stratification, antithetic variables, control variates and common random numbers; conditional models and the Gaussian, Student t, Clayton, Gumbel and Frank copulas; nine processes from Brownian motion to the Hawkes and variance-gamma processes with their stationarity, stability, explosion, boundary and discretisation conditions, sample paths and ensemble bands; the Euler time discretisation and multilevel Monte Carlo with the bias apart from the Monte Carlo error; a guided interview whose rule graph proposes candidate models with reasons, other explanations, rejection tests and sampling methods, can answer "insufficient evidence", and makes the same model record as the editor; a rare-event lab with valid exponential tilting (refused when E exp(θX) is infinite), multilevel splitting, subset simulation, adaptive importance sampling and the cross-entropy method on the tail of a sum, the Pollaczek–Khinchine ruin probability and a catastrophe and systemic ruin test with Hawkes arrivals, copula-linked shares, a cascade of defaults and three policies in light- and heavy-tailed regimes; a Philox4x32-10 generator with named streams and workers, exact or numerical reference values, claim tags for every result, and versioned model and run records. Four public-domain datasets: Bortkiewicz's horse kicks, Rutherford and Geiger's alpha particles, Weldon's dice and the annual rainfall maxima of Fort Collins. Works offline: MathJax 4.1.3 and Fira Math are embedded.
